content: Appropriate corrective and preventive actions must be implemented to address issues effectively. Regular in-service refresher training is essential to enhance the knowledge, skills, and attitudes of healthcare providers while also offering opportunities for support. Manufacturers of in vitro diagnostics (IVDs), or their economic operators (such as suppliers, distributors, or agents), are required to provide in-service training and troubleshooting support when product issues or adverse events arise. Authorities should consider developing national curricula for HIV testing and other aspects of HIV care and treatment, tailored to various testing settings. Certification of testing providers should also be considered as an incentive to reinforce the quality of HIV testing activities. In Brazil, the use of technology in training the healthcare workforce has significantly increased the coverage of HIV testing. The Brazilian Ministry of Health has prioritized expanding access to HIV diagnosis, particularly through rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs), as part of its strategy to achieve the 90–90–90 targets by 2020. In 2017, the ministry distributed over 12 million RDTs, a 23-fold increase compared to 2005 when RDTs were first adopted as a public health policy. To meet the growing demand, the number of healthcare workers trained to conduct HIV testing using RDTs was increased. Given the vast size of the country, with 5,570 cities, and the challenges of on-site training, a free distance-learning course called TELELAB was introduced. TELELAB offers online courses on sexually transmitted infection (STI) diagnosis, including video lessons and instruction manuals. For areas with limited internet access, the course is available on DVD by mail. Upon completing the course and passing an exam with a score of 70% or higher, professionals receive certification. Notably, 61% of certified providers are nurses. In 1,943 municipalities observed, 72% of healthcare professionals resided outside the capital, many in remote and rural areas without access to laboratory services. TELELAB has improved access to HIV diagnosis by enabling healthcare professionals, especially nurses, to enhance their HIV testing skills. This initiative has allowed the Ministry of Health to increase the annual distribution of RDTs. Building on its success, TELELAB is set to expand nationwide through a mobile phone application. Pre-market assessment of IVDs is a critical component of health systems, directly influencing the quality of HIV testing. The level of scrutiny during pre-market review depends on the product's risk classification, the country's needs, available resources, and the implementation of a national regulatory framework. Pre-market assessment, as mandated by national regulations or legislation, is a necessary step before authorizing the marketing of IVDs, including those for HIV. This process involves evaluating product quality, safety, and performance. However, many countries lack the legal framework or resources for effective IVD regulation. To address this gap, the World Health Organization (WHO) conducts prequalification assessments of IVDs likely to be used in resource-limited settings, particularly point-of-care diagnostics. WHO independently reviews the quality, safety, and performance of these IVDs and encourages national programs to prioritize WHO-prequalified IVDs during pre-market approval and product selection for national testing algorithms. The WHO prequalification process involves a standardized procedure to determine if a product meets its requirements, including a review of safety and performance data, inspection of the manufacturer's quality management system, and independent evaluation of performance and operational characteristics. Post-market surveillance is essential to monitor and detect any quality, safety, or performance issues with IVDs once they are on the market. While all stakeholders (end-users, manufacturers, regulators, and testing laboratories) have specific roles, the ultimate responsibility lies with the manufacturer, who relies on feedback, primarily through complaint reporting. WHO has issued specific guidance on post-market surveillance of IVDs. Reactive post-market surveillance occurs when an adverse event has already affected an individual being tested, the testing provider, or others nearby. For example, a false-negative test result may be reported if an individual is diagnosed elsewhere and presents for retesting. Proactive post-market surveillance aims to identify product problems before they result in adverse effects, such as through lot testing of random HIV RDT samples or reviewing scientific literature on similar products. When a problem is detected or an adverse event is reported, the manufacturer must record it in their complaint system and initiate their complaint-handling procedure. This includes reassessing the potential risk associated with continued use of the IVD. If the risk is deemed unacceptably high, the manufacturer may take corrective action, such as recalling a faulty lot of RDTs. End-users are often the first to detect issues with products at testing sites and should report problems to manufacturers and economic operators. National authorities, such as regulatory bodies and reference laboratories, may also support complaint reporting and conduct post-market surveillance as their capacity allows. WHO manages a complaint-reporting system for IVDs, emphasizing products recommended for use by WHO. End-users are encouraged to use standardized WHO forms to report complaints, including false-negative or false-positive results, invalid results, or visual defects. WHO oversees the investigation conducted by the manufacturer and any resulting corrective actions. If quality issues are not addressed promptly and adequately, the IVD may be removed from the list of WHO-prequalified products. Adverse events associated with IVDs can cause direct or indirect harm. Direct harm includes death or serious health deterioration, while indirect harm, such as misdiagnosis, delayed diagnosis, or absence of treatment, is more common with IVDs. National authorities should collaborate with professional external quality assessment (EQA) providers to build capacity for proficiency testing of their services, including addressing issues identified through quality activities. EQA is a valuable tool for post-market surveillance and identifying testing sites prone to errors that could lead to HIV misdiagnosis. Testing sites should participate in EQA schemes as frequently as possible, ideally at least once a year. Procurement and supply chain management of IVDs for national HIV testing programs vary by setting. In many countries, national authorities conduct centralized procurement for testing sites. In other settings, implementing partners such as NGOs and donors may assist with procurement and apply their quality assurance policies. This includes using testing algorithm verification studies to justify product selection. Accreditation of testing sites involves recognizing their quality and competence. National or international accreditation bodies assess whether a site's quality management system is functional and complies with established standards, such as ISO 15189 for medical laboratories. National authorities should consider moving toward accreditation of testing sites within their tiered networks. Quality management systems must be applied to all services conducting HIV testing and diagnosis, whether facility-based or community-based. Site supervisors are responsible for quality activities and should be trained in quality management principles. Quality should be an integral part of the roles and responsibilities of all staff members, not a one-time activity or the responsibility of a single individual.
